paragraphs.text: Revelation: a vision, or the disclosure of a mystery, or the manifestation of the will of God.
Jesus Christ: that is, the Lord Jesus is the source of this revelation and no one else.
Which God gave unto him: the Father loves mankind and sent His Son to redeem them, and the Son has all that belongs to the Father, including the revelation to mankind and their judgment as well.
Shortly: this does not mean a specific time, as some have understood; for "one day is with the Lord as a thousand years" (2 Pet 3:8).
By his angel: he is the means of conveying the message, and in fact there was more than one angel who exchanged the revelations during the book.

St. John begins to convey his vision to us by affirming that what he saw is a prophetic vision which he saw while awake and not a dream during his sleep. He affirms that the source of this vision is the Lord Jesus, and its purpose is "to shew unto his servants," that is, that God makes known His will to His beloved children, and God used one of His servants (the angels) to convey this revelation to St. John.
The words here all refer to St. John, who bore witness to Christ by his preaching, his Gospel and his three Epistles, in addition to what he saw and recorded in this book as well.
Blessed: that is, how happy!

St. John urges and encourages the believers to read and listen to the content of this prophecy, to meditate on it and remember its meanings by keeping them in the heart and doing them; and in his encouragement he reminds the believers of what he said earlier, that the time is at hand.

May you show others the importance of the word of God in the Holy Bible, and the importance of attending church and enjoying its teachings and sacraments, because the crowding of material life keeps them busy and away from it; and be sure that when you encourage others, you are refreshed first and are encouraged, and your attachment to the Church increases.

entries.section: (2) The address to the seven churches

paragraphs.text: The seven churches: these are the most famous churches that were established and settled at that time in the region of present-day Turkey, and they will be mentioned in detail in the following chapters; they also signify the whole Church in every time and place.

Which is, and which was: this expression was used for the first time in God's declaration of Himself to the prophet Moses in (Ex 3:14) when He said "I AM THAT I AM"; and because this expression signifies the divine Self, it is a declaration concerning God the Father.

The seven Spirits: this declaration is also from the one Holy Spirit; the expression "seven" does not mean plurality but means the perfection and diversity of the gifts and endowments of the Holy Spirit.

St. John begins his address to the seven churches with the usual Christian greeting "Grace and peace," which is a petition and prayer more than a greeting, and he makes clear that the source of all grace and peace is God the Father, the eternal and everlasting, and the Holy Spirit.

entries.section: (2) The address to the seven churches

paragraphs.text: From Jesus Christ: that is, He too is a source of grace and peace, like the Father and the Holy Spirit (that is, the whole Holy Trinity). The faithful witness: that is, by His life on earth Christ was a faithful witness to the Father (Jn 18:37), and by His resurrection He bore witness to His divinity, which death cannot overcome.
The firstborn from the dead: that is, the first who raised Himself by Himself, and His resurrection was without a second death.

This verse completes what came in the previous verse, that Christ is the source of grace and peace; but John goes on here to bring out some of Christ's attributes, in that by His life, His death and His resurrection He became a faithful witness to everything He said about Himself, about His Father and about the Holy Spirit. Among His attributes also is that He is above every rule and authority, "the prince of the kings of the earth," and that He expressed His love by His Incarnation and by redeeming us with His most holy Blood, in which is the forgiveness of our sins, and we receive His power in the sacraments of the Church, the first of which is the washing with the water of Baptism. The word firstborn also means that He is the firstborn of all the people whom He brings with Him into Paradise and the Kingdom, for He is the "firstborn among many brethren" (Rom 8:29).

entries.section: (2) The address to the seven churches

paragraphs.text: And has made us - Christ - spiritual kings who reign over our will, which was formerly overcome, and priests who offer to Him ourselves as living sacrifices pleasing before Him by striving in the commandment, and by offering the sacrifices of prayer and praise also to God, the possessor of all glory, honor and dominion.
May we examine ourselves before every action: is it fitting that this deed should come from a king or a priest?!

entries.section: (2) The address to the seven churches

paragraphs.text: With clouds: the cloud signifies the glory of God (Mt 24:30), and also the fear of Him (Ps 97:2, 3); therefore in the Divine Liturgy, when we remember the coming of the Lord Christ, we say of Him, "Fearful and full of glory."

Every eye: an expression that carries us from the limits of material place to spiritual measures that men cannot comprehend, so that wherever a person is on the globe, he will see this awesome coming.
Here is a reference to the second coming of Christ which was mentioned in (Acts 1:11), and a description of the state of those who await His coming, and they are two groups...
The first: the righteous, whose hearts are attached to His coming and who await it, and His coming will be for them the secret of their happiness and the beginning of their eternal inheritance.

As for the second group: they are those who "pierced him... and shall wail," that is, the Jews who crucified Him, pierced Him and rejected Him, as well as all the world that still rejects Him or has become Christian in name only; and the wailing here is an expression of grief, dread and regret which will not profit its owner at that time.

entries.section: (2) The address to the seven churches

paragraphs.text: One of the strongest verses that prove the divinity of Christ...

Alpha and Omega: a comparison in the form of a metaphor that becomes clearer in the following phrase "the beginning and the ending"; just as the letters of a language have a first letter and a last, so God is the first and source of everything and the end and last of everything, so that nothing is before Him and nothing is after Him, and this is what we express theologically as the eternity and everlastingness of God. Which is, and which was: an expression that indicates the divine Self, "the hypostasis of the Father," as in (Ex 3:14) when God declared Himself to Moses in the same words, and here the same expression is used of Christ "the Son" also, because afterward He said "which is to come," which pertains to Christ alone.
The Almighty: proof of His divinity, in that He is the Creator and the Sustainer of all.
The speaker makes clear that He is the eternal, everlasting Christ, who became incarnate in the fullness of time, and the Almighty, that is, He is God.

My beloved brother: the scene of the second coming of Christ is a terrible and awesome scene; our holy Fathers kept it before their eyes and so their lives became upright, while others ignored it and were overcome by their lusts, and each group has a destiny entirely different from the other. A question, my friend, that I put to myself along with you... where do we stand?

entries.section: (3) The state of John and his call to the vision

paragraphs.text: I John.. your brother: St. John declares his name here, which is necessary to gain confidence and to affirm that he is the source of all his words that follow; and he added the word your brother, although he is one of the twelve pure Apostles, as a kind of humility of a father with his children when he condescends to them.

Your companion in tribulation: the Church had begun its journey of suffering with the Roman persecution and the martyrdom of many, that is, it was in severe tribulation, and John was in tribulation of another kind, for he was exiled to "the isle called Patmos," a Greek island, in the reign of the Emperor "Domitian"; and the saint wanted his children to feel heartfelt support for them and to encourage them, for he bears tribulation as they do, and to increase their hope he also reminds them that they are all partakers in the glory of "the kingdom of Jesus Christ."
For the testimony: that is, the cause of this tribulation is our witness and our preaching in the name of Christ, and for this reason the tribulation is at the same time the cause of our boasting.

The writer of the book repeats that he is John because of the importance of knowing the source of every word mentioned in it, and he also makes clear that he shares with the Church, in his time and in every time, the tribulations through which it passes, since he was exiled on the island of Patmos for the sake of Christ.

entries.section: (3) The state of John and his call to the vision

paragraphs.text: I was in the Spirit: this is the state in which St. John received the vision, and it is like what Paul declared in (2 Cor 12:2) about his own vision, and what Peter likewise declared in (Acts 10:10); it is a state above every known material sense, for in it a person is wholly subject to the Holy Spirit, and so, as if in absence, he sees and hears what no one else sees or hears. The Lord's day: that is, this happened on a Sunday. And everything began when he heard a loud voice, as of a trumpet, coming from behind him, and the trumpet means a warning or caution of approaching danger..

St. John shows that the vision was on Sunday and that he was in a spiritual state as if absent from the material things around him, although he was awake, and he heard a loud voice alerting him like the sound of a trumpet.

entries.section: (3) The state of John and his call to the vision

paragraphs.text: I am Alpha and Omega: the one who spoke began by identifying Himself to John by one of His attributes that show His divinity, namely eternity and everlastingness (see the explanation of v. 8).

What thou seest... write: after the identification came the direct command from the speaker - God the Son - to St. John, a specific commission that he write all that he would see in a book and send this book to the seven churches which were mentioned before in (v. 4), although here the speaker added their names, which will be discussed in detail in the next two chapters.
The speaker declared that He is God and commanded him to write all that he sees and to send it to the seven churches of Asia Minor.

If you have been heedless of some matters necessary for your salvation and have cast them behind your back, and then God alerts you to them through someone around you, such as talk about prayer or fasting or almsgiving, do not neglect the words, because they are the word of God sent to you personally, and quickly decide what you will begin with.

The Apostle John turned around toward the source of the speaker's voice and saw seven golden lampstands. The golden lampstand was known to the Jews, since it was among the furnishings of the Tabernacle of Meeting, and God commanded that it be made to give light in the sanctuary (Ex 25:31); but here St. John makes clear to us that they signify the seven churches (v. 20), for the Church in God's sight is the lampstand that gives light to the world in its darkness, and it is of gold because gold signifies the purity of the believers who are the very Body of Christ, and gold also signifies the kingship, that is, the authority of the Church over the world.
John describes the Christ who appeared to him, and in this verse and the following verses he recounts His attributes, which are:

1- The Son of man: a title that Christ gave Himself during His Incarnation, and it is a title that indicates His complete humanity; it is also to be noted that Daniel in his vision of Christ mentioned this very title (Dan 7:13).

2- Clothed with a garment down to the foot: like the garments of the high priest, and this is the second attribute that John presents to us of Christ in his vision, for He is first the incarnate Son of man and second the High Priest of our confession (Heb 5:5); as for the golden girdle, it points to His kingship and His everlasting authority.

St. John continues describing the appearance of Christ, and it is to be noted here that the form of Christ differs from His usual appearance to us, which is fixed in our minds from His Incarnation, because the emphasis here is rather on His attributes and His divinity.

3- His head and his hairs were white: the color white always signifies purity, cleanness and holiness, and when hair is described as white it is a reference to the wisdom of the elders, and it also signifies the antiquity and eternity of Christ.

4- His eyes were as a flame of fire: that is, the penetration of His insight, for He alone knows and searches the hidden things of men's hearts, and it also means the justice of God and His firmness, and His not being lenient with sin or the wicked.
5- His feet like unto fine brass: Daniel mentioned in his vision "his feet like in colour to polished brass"

(Dan 10:6). The fine or polished brass is brass to which a little gold or silver has been added to increase its brightness; so His feet point to strength and firmness and the union of divinity with humanity in the one nature of Christ. It can also be said that the word His feet represents the two attributes of justice and mercy in God's rule and in His judgment of mankind.
6- His voice as the sound of many waters: that is, His voice is deep and awesome, and it is like the waters that bring good, fruitfulness and blessings to everyone they reach.
7- His right hand: signifies strength, care and leadership.
The seven stars: that is, the seven bishops responsible for the seven churches (v. 20).

8- A sword.. twoedged: that is, His words that go out of His mouth, which have the power of the sword that pierces to the depths of the soul and spirit (Heb 4:12). The two edges also signify the Old and the New Testament.

St. John continues the description of the Master, and sees Him holding the seven bishops in His right hand, showing His authority and power over them on the one hand, and their enjoyment of His protection and guidance on the other. It can also be said that they are instruments in the hand of God to declare His purpose and will to the Church.
And His words are decisive and penetrating, whether in the Old Testament or the New Testament (the two edges of the sword).
9- His countenance was as the sun shineth: this signifies the beauty and splendor of His face and the glory of His divinity, which none can approach.

From the intensity of the splendor, beauty and majesty of the indescribable sight, John fell in fear, as dead, at His feet; but Christ in His tenderness touched him with His pure hand, and with His calm, reassuring voice encouraged him, saying, Fear not; then Christ declares His divinity by saying "the first and the last," that is, I am the eternal, everlasting God, as came in v. 8.

My beloved God: how awesome, wonderful and heavenly was what St. John saw, so that he fell as dead, and so both Isaiah and Ezekiel shared with him when they saw You in their visions (Isa 6:5), (Ezek 10); but I complain of myself to You, my Master, for I still do not feel Your majesty and Your fear when I stand before You, and often laziness and slackness overcome me in my prayer because I forget the glory of the One before whom I stand... I beseech You, my God, forgive me and plant Your fear in my flesh and in my heart.
Christ declares Himself more clearly to John, and to us also, saying of Himself:

I am he that liveth: it comes in the continuous tense, that is, I was living and am still living, and am the source and giver of life; and it is to be noted that this title is among the attributes of God Himself (Mt 16:16, Rom 9:26). And was dead: that is, I passed through death and tasted it in the body, and this is what John knows well about the person of Christ.
For evermore: an affirmation of the eternity of God.

Have the keys of hell and of death: hell (Hades) is the place where the wicked wait after their death (the abode of the dead), and the keys mean the absolute authority of Christ over these souls and over the place itself; and besides declaring His authority, we can understand Christ's saying here to mean that He encourages His children and removes from them the specter of the fear of hell, since He conquered and opened its gates once and brought out all the souls that were awaiting His redemption; and therefore this verse is considered one of the strongest verses that express the divinity of Christ and prove it beyond the slightest doubt, for He is the eternal, everlasting One (v. 17), and He became incarnate and died and rose, and He has authority over Hades as we explained before, and these are matters that cannot apply except to God alone..., so Christ is therefore God Himself.
Write the things which thou hast seen: that is, what John saw from the beginning of the revelation, and the attributes of Christ, in the first chapter.
And the things which are: in the present time, and these are the events relating to the seven churches, and they occupy the second and third chapters.

And the things which shall be hereafter: that is, the following and future prophecies, which will happen throughout the ages until the end and eternity, and they occupy from the fourth chapter to the end of the book.

At the end of the chapter St. John explains what a person cannot grasp by himself, making clear to us that the seven stars are the bishops of the seven churches and that the seven lampstands are the seven churches themselves.

Angel: the divine inspiration used the word angel to express the bishops of the churches. And the word angel in its origin and meaning is the servant sent by God to convey a message to mankind... and so we learn that God describes the stewards of His mysteries as angels, because of the majesty and importance of the work of the priesthood in His Church.

The letters to the first four churches, a general introduction to the seven churches: it is fitting for us here, before entering into the letters addressed to the seven churches, to clarify some matters and characteristics relating to these churches.
First: these letters were addressed to the seven churches in Asia Minor (Turkey), but they are divine pastoral letters addressed to the Church in every time and every place.

Second: all the letters were addressed to the name of the bishop "the angel of the church" because he is responsible before God for the service of His Church; but in the spiritual meaning the letter is addressed to every servant, indeed to all the people also, for the healing of spiritual sicknesses.
Third: there are general characteristics shared by these letters, such as:
1- All the letters began with the imperative verb "Write unto..." and this command was of course addressed to John.

2- "These things saith" is repeated in all the letters and it is a reference to the Lord Christ; then it is followed by one of the attributes of the Lord that suits the state of the church to which He addresses the letter, as will become clear in the interpretation.

3- The repetition of expressions such as "I know" before beginning the discourse, and the phrase "He that hath an ear, let him hear" after the counsel and warning, and the expression "He that overcometh" before the promise of a reward for the one who overcomes.

"Ephesus": the capital of the province of Asia Minor at that time. Its church was founded by St. Paul and then became a center for the ministry of St. John as well. It was famous because it was a seaport and because of the famous pagan temple of "Artemis" there, and it was known for its corruption and at first for its resistance to Christianity. It gradually lost its fame after the center of Christianity moved to Constantinople in the fourth century, and it was completely destroyed by the Turks in the fourteenth century.

"The angel of the church": there is no certainty about the person of the bishop of this church, but he is one of two persons and no third: either St. Timothy, the disciple of the Apostle Paul, or the bishop "Onesimus" mentioned in the letters of St. Ignatius.
"He that holdeth... who walketh": see the explanation of (ch. 1:13-16); the reference here is to the authority and care of the Lord Christ for the bishops and the churches.

I know thy works and thy labour: the Lord Christ begins by presenting Himself with the attribute of "the One who knows," that is, the One who searches and knows everything, an attribute we must always remember... for remembering it reminds us of the just judgment if we neglect, and gives us hope that every labor and struggle offered for God's sake is not forgotten before Him. Thy patience: a testimony from Christ to the striving, patience and endurance of His servant.
Thou canst not bear: another praise from the Lord Christ to this bishop, that his soul cannot bear to be reconciled with the wicked, or to go along with them or agree with them in their evil.

Hast tried: that is, you examined their claim, their preaching and their false pretensions that they were Christians, and found them to be infiltrating Jews whose whole aim was to destroy the Christian faith.

He praises the angel of the church for his service and his labors in it, his patient endurance of tribulations, his rejection of the words of the wicked and his care in examining the false teachers in order to expose their false teachings.
He continues praising the bishop in the previous verse, and adds a new attribute, that he "hast not fainted."
This is the attribute of perseverance in service, which does not know or acknowledge frustration and despair.

This bishop was distinguished by labor in service and patience in tribulations. May you not grumble at the abundance of responsibilities or at others troubling you, for your labor is very precious to God and He will reward you for it, so persevere in it for His sake.

After the Lord Christ praised His bishop for the virtues he enjoyed in his pastoral life, He begins to direct a rebuke to him, and may we learn this quality from the Lord Christ, which He used with all the bishops, because it carries much gentleness and sensitivity toward the other, and it is praise before reproof. I have somewhat against thee: that is, there is something held against you and for which you are condemned.

Thou hast left thy first love: this is the sickness of this church or of its bishop; with the abundance of work, service, problems and wars, the feelings of his first love for Christ were lost, and lukewarmness and routine entered the spiritual life, a sickness that a person may not feel but which before God is a great evil, for "if a man would give all the substance of his house for love, it would utterly be contemned" (Song 8:7).
The Lord Christ goes straight into the remedy....

Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent: return to yourself and examine it, and search for the causes of the beginning of this fall in your love toward Me, and when you grasp these causes you can offer a true repentance in order to avoid what made you fall into this sickness... and the Lord Christ teaches us in the parable of the prodigal son that repentance and return began with an examination of the soul, "he came to himself" (Lk 15:17), which the Church also makes us aware of and teaches us.
Take care to set aside a few minutes in which you sit with God and your soul before meeting your father of confession, so that your repentance may be sound.

And do the first works: return to what you used to do before with love, and perhaps what is meant here is the works of the inner chamber, such as fervent prayer that kindles the heart with the love of God.

I will come unto thee quickly...: the second coming is not what is meant, but rather a warning of an earthly punishment for the one who does not repent or does not respond to the warning, for God, in His love and tenderness toward His creation, is also just and corrects those who do not repent, and so He sometimes allows them an earthly punishment if this benefits them. And remove thy candlestick: that is, your position as a bishop or servant, since you ought to have been a light to your people. The lampstand also comes to mean the Church, and if the Church does not repent of its sin, such as its concern for administrative matters at the expense of spiritual matters and the love of God, its destiny too will be to vanish.

He gives him a solution to his problem, which is quick repentance and a return to his first worship and services with care and fervor, and He warns him that if he does not repent He will punish him and he will lose his standing with God, and his service may be taken from him.
After the Lord Christ's severe blame and His presentation of the decisive remedy for this church and its bishop, He returns to encourage before He concludes His words....
But this thou hast: that is, it is counted to your credit... and it is the opposite of the expression "I have somewhat against thee."

The deeds of the Nicolaitans: they are the followers of "Nicolas," one of the seven deacons (Acts 6:5), and it was attributed to them that they permitted "fornication..."!! and gluttony in pleasures without restraint, and for this reason the Church excommunicated them, but they found a place in "Ephesus," and for this reason the bishop resisted and rebuked them.
Here He returned and encouraged him for his exactness in the faith and his rejection of the heretics, who are the Nicolaitans.

Christ rejoices when He finds His servant hating what He does not love... and this statement is for all of us; therefore, my God, we ask Your Holy Spirit to work in us with power so that our will may be united with Your will, and we do not do or make anything contrary to Your pleasure or without Your will.

He that hath an ear, let him hear: an expression the Lord used with the churches, and its meaning is that one must hear the voice and act upon it, and that whoever ignores the word of God is like the deaf man who has no ears.

What the Spirit saith: that is, what the Lord Christ declared in His vision to John, the Holy Spirit also declares to the churches in every time and place, and these declarations, as we said before, must be obeyed and carried out. To him that overcometh: an expression that is also repeated, and it is rich in its meanings:
(1) That is, the possibility of victory and overcoming is available to all believers and is not difficult as long as they love and obey God.

(2) That defeat goes back to the person himself if he rejects the commandment and the work of the Holy Spirit in his life. (3) That there are some who may lose everything, whatever their standing in the Church; salvation is not guaranteed to a person as long as he does not safeguard it by constant repentance and spiritual striving, even if he is a bishop. The tree of life: points to Christ Himself, as the most precious reward for the one who overcomes, who enjoys being satisfied with Him in Paradise and eternal life, and the phrase "in the midst of the paradise" points to the presence of Christ in the midst of all His children, and that the sight of Him will be available to all.
He calls him to obey these words addressed to him and encourages him with the reward he will receive, which is to be satisfied with Christ in eternity.

Smyrna: a city lying north of Ephesus, a port on the Aegean Sea, famous for trade and wealth; today it is known by the name of the Turkish city (Izmir)... Its bishop was the martyr "Polycarp," the disciple of St. John the Apostle, and the church of Smyrna is the only church that the Lord Christ did not rebuke for a clear fault like the rest of the churches, but His letter to it was rather a letter of encouragement.
The first and the last... was dead, and is alive: see the explanation of ch. 1:11, 17, 18.

Since the church of Smyrna was a church suffering from persecution and torments unto death, the Lord here presents Himself as the eternal, everlasting God so that it may make light of the temporary sufferings, because its God lifts it above temporal sufferings and gives it eternal life; and He is also a conqueror who passed through death and defeated it by the Resurrection, to give the Church comfort that He suffered before as it suffers now, so He shares with it and it imitates Him; likewise He gives it hope that after death there is life and after persecution eternal happiness.

I know thy works, and tribulation: a word of encouragement for the bishop and the church: all your labor and endurance are before Me, and I never forget the labor of love or the endurance of tribulations for My name's sake.
And poverty: that is, your material poverty in the midst of the rich city of Smyrna, and it is one of the tribulations through which the church passed.
But thou art rich: but what the world sees in you as poverty I see as riches, for you are rich in your sound faith and your example to your church.

The blasphemy of them which say they are...: here the Lord makes clear to us that the first thorn of persecution was from the Jews who resisted Christianity violently, believing by that that they were true Jews pleasing God, but Christ describes everyone who persecutes His Church as a synagogue of Satan.

My dear friend... which is more important to you... to be rich in the sight of God or in the world by its material measures? May we be poor in the world but rich toward God... for just as material wealth has many wars, so spiritual wealth has many blessings; only then do we understand the saying of the Apostle Paul, "as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things" (2 Cor 6:10). So care for your spiritual life and do not be troubled by financial tribulations, however much those around you grow rich.

Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer: the Lord Christ increases His encouragement of the Church and His support of it, and affirms that the suffering will continue for another period, and He also reveals to us that Satan, in his envy and fury, is the one who plans the persecution of the new Church so that its faith may perish; but the Church must not fear as long as Christ supports it in its sufferings, even if Satan in his first rounds is able to cast some of them into prison.

Ten days: the expression here is symbolic and does not indicate its literal meaning but expresses shortness; what is meant is that, despite the severity of the tribulation, it will be limited in duration, especially when compared with the unlimited glories of eternity.

The Lord Christ increases His encouragement of the bishop of this church by urging him: Be thou faithful, to stand firm in the faith to the end of life, for the reward is great in return when God crowns him with the crown of happiness in eternal life. That God may remove the harshness of the trial from him, He let him know that it is temporary and encouraged him to continue holding fast to his faith and his faithfulness in his life, because He has prepared for him a great crown in heaven.

The second death: the first death is the death of the body, which all men will pass through, but the second death is spiritual death and eternal perdition, a death that does not touch the believers who obtain the crown of life; and this is what the Lord said of it, "If a man keep my saying, he shall never see death" (Jn 8:51). St. John will explain more about this subject in the twentieth chapter when he speaks of the millennial kingdom.

Much suffering and persecution wears on the souls of many, so that they leave the way... but relying on the divine promises and remembering them casts out fear and frustration and renews the spirit of perseverance, striving and endurance... so grant us, our God, to pass through the second death to the crown of life, not disturbed by the lightness of temporary tribulations, for they are a cause of blessing and work for us a weight of eternal glory...

The bishop of the church here is the martyr Carpus, as the historian Eusebius mentioned. Pergamos: it lay on a high mountain and was famous for its library, its abundant cultures and its philosophical schools. He which hath the sharp sword with two edges: since this church was known for lack of exactness and for being influenced by many of the ideas around it, the Lord Christ presented Himself here in the image of the decisive judge, whose word is conclusive and divides between what is true in the faith and what is false (see ch. 1:16, and see also the explanation of v. 16).

Where thou dwellest... where Satan's seat is: the Lord Christ affirms, as He affirmed to all the churches, that He knows the conditions and circumstances of every church, and Pergamos in particular was famous for its pagan worship, since it had many pagan temples, such as the temple of Zeus, the temple of Minerva, the temple of Apollo, and the worship of Asclepius, the god of medicine, and for this reason it deserved the title seat of Satan.

Thou holdest fast my name: praise of the bishop of Pergamos, who, despite the strength of the opposing current, did not deny his faith even in the worst days of persecution, which reached martyrdom, as happened with "Antipas," who died burned, refusing compromises, so that he deserved to be called by the Lord "my faithful martyr..."

Notice, beloved, that all we know about "Antipas," this faithful martyr, is only a few lines written by the historian Andreas; but God does not forget anyone's labor, and He praises this martyr and mentions him in His holy book... so do not care to be known among men, but to be praised by God, who sees in secret and rewards openly.
I have a few things against thee: a gentle rebuke that is not without firmness, and it is also considered an introduction to diagnosing the sickness of the church.

The doctrine of Balaam: Balaam was a prophet who lived among the Gentiles, and when the kings of the Gentiles feared the people of the children of Israel coming from the wilderness of Sinai to take their lands, they hired Balaam to curse them, but God prevented him from doing so. And before the offers of money presented by "Balak," king of Moab, Balaam weakened, and he did not curse the people of God, but at the same time he deceived God, for he told "Balak" that if this people sinned by fornication their God would be angry with them and leave them, and this is what "Balak" actually did by presenting the Moabite women as a stumblingblock to the people of Israel, and they committed fornication with them and Balak triumphed over them (see the Book of Numbers, chs. 22-25)... The meaning intended here is that in the church of "Pergamos" there were people who incited the believing Christians to take part in the feasts of what was sacrificed to idols, which would be the beginning of the stumblingblock and God's wrath upon them.
The teaching here is for all of us, so we must avoid all the stumblingblocks with which Satan bargains with us, lest he separate us from God.
Likewise, in the church of Pergamos there were other people who held the teachings of Nicolas, which were discussed before in (v. 6).

Repent: always returning, and the beginning is by repentance, and He mentioned the quick coming as a kind of warning as He did with the church of Ephesus (v. 5). I will fight against them with the sword of my mouth: that is, I will resist them and destroy them by the power of My word, for I will raise up faithful servants and preachers and put My word in their mouths, and no one will be able to stand before them...

He that hath an ear, let him hear: see the explanation of (v. 7). To him that overcometh... the hidden manna: victory and overcoming are always the condition for the reward, and the reward here is "the hidden manna."

The manna: it is the food that God gave to His people in the wilderness to sustain them (Ex 16...); in the New Testament it is the living Body of Christ which we receive in the Eucharist, and whoever eats it lives forever (Jn 6:33, 50, 51). In eternity the meaning is the constant fellowship with Christ, since Christ becomes our only food. A white stone: this is the second reward after "the manna," and the color white is a metaphor for purity and cleanness, while the expression white stone has a historical background... for it was the custom in the Greek and Roman courts that a white stone was given to acquit the accused and a black stone when he was condemned, and the name of the accused was engraved on the white stone, and he carried it with him always as proof of his innocence...; so also the Lord gives everyone who overcomes a declaration of his righteousness and of his victory that all can see.

A new name written, which no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it: the talk in the Book of Revelation about heaven is tied to everything that is new: "the new Jerusalem" (ch. 3:12), "my new name" (ch. 3:12), the new song (ch. 5:9), the new heaven (ch. 21:1), and all things new (ch. 21:5). The new name here means... the particularity of the relationship between each person who strove and overcame and the Lord Christ, as when a father gives his son a pet name that is not given to any other of his children.
Whoever hears and obeys the word of God, He will give him constant satisfaction in heaven, a pure life, a personal relationship with Him and an inexpressible enjoyment.

My beloved brother, the Lord's encouragement of us and His gifts are beyond all description, for the delight of His heart is in the gifts of His inheritance which He prepared for us beforehand... so do not let any negligence, laziness, preoccupation, slackness or lack of exactness rob you of what your Christ has prepared for you.
The angel of the church: he is the bishop St. "Irenaeus," the disciple of St. Polycarp, who was famous for fervor of spirit.

Thyatira: a city lying between Pergamos and Sardis, famous for the worship of "Apollo," the sun god, and for the trade in purple, and it is the town of "Lydia," the seller of purple, and it was said that the sin of this church was flattery at the expense of the truth.
The Son of God: a strong declaration by Christ of His divinity, after He used in His Incarnation the expression Son of man to indicate His humanity.

Eyes like unto a flame of fire: Christ here presents Himself in a way that suits the state of the church, as we will see later, but the attribute of the eyes here means that He is the One who searches everything, who examines every matter, who exposes crooked sinners, and nothing is hidden from Him.

His feet are like fine brass: that is, the purity and clarity of His teaching - the sound faith - and it can also be said, His strength, that is, He is like the brass that crushes His enemies like vessels of pottery.
Christ presents Himself to the church of Thyatira, which flatters at the expense of the truth, as the just God who searches everything, and His teachings are the strong truth which shatters all evil.

I know... this church and this bishop were distinguished by love, faith, service in the fullness of its giving, endurance, longsuffering and spiritual growth, so the Lord testified to him that the last works are more than the first, but the most important thing that distinguishes him is that he did not lose his first love (v. 4) like the bishop of the church of Ephesus.
I have a few things against thee: that is, he also fell into a fault, and the word "a few" perhaps means without intending it.

Thou sufferest that woman Jezebel: she is a rich person who entered the church and served in it, and we do not know whether her real name was Jezebel or whether it is a name God gave her because of her likeness to Jezebel the wicked queen, the wife of Ahab king of Israel, whose evil reached its utmost..

As for this woman, because of the church's flattery of her for her wealth, she began to claim knowledge - a prophetess - and to teach the simple people to eat things sacrificed to idols, which the Church forbade (Acts 15:29), and to seduce them also to fornication, and the fornication here may be in its spiritual meaning, that is, the distortion of their faith.
I gave her space to repent: here the Lord reveals to us His longsuffering with sinners, that perhaps they may use it for their repentance.
I will cast her into a bed: that is, I will punish her either with sickness or with what hinders her and paralyzes her movement.

Them that commit adultery with her: that is, her disciples and followers and those who flatter her and agree with her, will have a punishment too, and Christ describes the punishment as being a tribulation great in its severity.

Death and eternal perdition will be the destiny of everyone who went along with her, and My punishment will be an example to the rest of the churches, which will know and be sure that I am the just God who searches the depths of the soul, and that although I delay with sinners, My punishment is just and I reward every person according to his works.

Because God is just in His judgments, He does not take anyone for another's fault, and for this reason He separates between the one who followed evil and deserved punishment and the one who kept himself away from strange teachings, so that God does not bring upon him anything of this.
The depths of Satan: an expression meaning experiencing evil to its very end.
Other burden: that is, I do not demand of them anything beyond their ability.

As for the teaching and sound faith that you have, hold it fast with strength and avoid the deviant ideas of faith until the last days and the end of creation by My coming, because everyone who strives and overcomes by his steadfastness in the faith and by keeping My commandments and doing them, I will give him of My power and My authority; for just as I possess everything, I give My children also a spiritual kingship over the souls of those who are far off (the Gentiles), that is, they can influence them and draw them to the faith.
By this authority they shepherd them with spiritual care and lead them (those far from the faith) into the fold of the faith.
A rod of iron: a symbol of strength, authority and firmness in leadership and guidance.

As the vessels of a potter shall they be broken to shivers: another image which, like the previous one, shows the strength of the authority of the children of God over the Gentiles or those who are far off, and to indicate also the strength of this given authority the Lord Christ adds another comparison, that just as the authority of the Son (Christ) was complete.. so will be the authority of those of His children who overcome.

The morning star: the Lord Christ declared at the end of the Book of Revelation that He Himself is "the bright and morning star" (ch. 22:16), that is, the most precious reward for the one who overcomes is to enjoy the possession of Christ Himself, that is, in eternity He gives Himself to each one of the heirs of His Kingdom.
See v. 7.

How wonderful is Your giving, Lord, and how wonderful is the beauty of eternity.. how can this be? How can we eat You, O tree of life, and how can we partake of You, O hidden manna, and how can we possess You, O morning star, unlimited in Your glory?! What John wrote is higher than the imagination of any human mind, but we trust in Your word and Your promises, so give us the spirit of striving that we may overcome and enjoy all that You have prepared for us, O Beloved of our souls.. my holy God.
Letters to the rest of the seven churches
The angel of the church: historians mention that the bishop of Sardis was St. Melito.
Sardis: a city on a mountain in the region of Asia Minor (Turkey), famous for its shops, its debauchery and its pagan worship associated with licentiousness, like the rest of the pagan lands.

The seven Spirits: that is, the One who has the Holy Spirit in fullness; see (ch. 1:4). The seven stars: the seven churches; see (ch. 1:20). The problem of this church or this bishop was the formality and outward show of worship, and for this reason he had a fame and a good reputation, "a name," so the Lord Christ presented Himself here with the theological attribute that suits the state of this church, for He is the One who searches the depths by His Holy Spirit and the One who has authority over all the churches. And the Lord exposes the sickness directly in order to hasten the remedy, and makes clear that the outward appearance does not deceive God even if it deceives men, but if a person remains in this state he is dead, that is, without life before God, and in perdition in eternity if he does not repent.

Be watchful: that is, awake and rise from what you are now drowning in, the deception of pride and your spiritual death, and hasten to rescue first the remainder of your life and then the rest of your people who have not died so far. Strengthen: that is, establish them, strengthen them and rescue them from death.
That are ready to die: that is, if you do not hasten to repent yourself and your people, the little goodness that remains in you will go away as well.

I have not found thy works perfect: that is, the measure is not what men praise you for in outward works but what I, God, examine and judge, and My judgment upon you is your neglect and your turning away from your spiritual striving; and it is also to be noted here that God's judgment and condemnation are on the works of a person, whether hidden or visible.

The words here are for all of us... for often we care about what we show before men and forget that God sees what is in secret, so that praise is our portion here, while rebuke and condemnation are God's judgment upon us... May we act upon the remedy that God presents to all of us and watch over our lives and our salvation, for they are the most precious things!!...

Remember how: that is, the remedy begins with your remembering your first feelings (ch. 2:4) in your love for God, and how your eagerness and first longings were when you first heard about faith in Me and received the fullness of the grace of the Holy Spirit in Baptism and the laying on of hands (the anointing of the Myron). Hold fast, and repent: that is, after you remember, you must take the next step, which is returning by repentance and putting My commandments into practice and doing them.

If therefore thou shalt not watch...: but if you remain in your negligence and your acceptance of praise and your outward worship. I will come on thee as a thief: just as a person does not know when the thief will come to steal from him, so I will come with My punishment quickly at a time you do not expect, [see also what the Lord Christ said about His second coming in (Mt 24:42, 25:5) about the need to watch, not knowing the hour, and the necessity of constant readiness.]

Thou hast a few names: although the sin of hypocrisy was widespread in this church, God in His justice does not take anyone for another's fault, and for this reason He declares plainly that there is a small number of true believers whom sin did not touch, since their conduct was pure (white garments), and their reward too will be to accompany Christ in eternity, "they shall walk with me," and Christ will declare their purity before all on the Day of Judgment.
He that overcometh, God will reward with the following:
1- He shall be clothed in white raiment: that is, he lives in purity with God forever.

2- I will not blot out his name out of the book of life: that is, he is established in the Kingdom of Heaven, and to explain this phrase further: we believe that when any person comes out of Baptism his name is written in the book of life, that is, the register of the heirs of the Kingdom of God, but the person by his faith, his striving and his works that please God is established in the inheritance of his heavenly Father, whereas he who was negligent and careless and did not watch over the salvation of his soul has his name removed from the inheritance of eternity.

3- I will confess his name before my Father: that is, the Lord Christ will declare in all of heaven "before my Father, and before his angels" the holiness of this person, his piety and his holding to pure conduct in his striving.
He that hath an ear: see (ch. 2:7).
The angel of the church: he is St. Quadratus.
Philadelphia: a city built by the king of Pergamos (Philadelphus) who gave it his name, and it was subject to many earthquakes that impoverished it and made its inhabitants abandon it over the ages.

He that is holy, he that is true: the Lord Christ presents Himself here by one of His names and attributes, "the Holy," an attribute that is applied to God alone and no one shares this title with Him, that is, a clear declaration of His divinity, and likewise He is "the True," that is, the One who searches the depths, truthful in His words and just in His judgments. He that hath the key of David: Isaiah prophesied of Christ the Savior and said, "And the key of the house of David will I lay upon his shoulder; so he shall open, and none shall shut; and he shall shut, and none shall open" (Isa 22:22). So the Lord Christ affirms here that He is the one of whom Isaiah spoke by the Holy Spirit, and the expression "the key of David" means the absolute authority of the King, in whose hand is everything, so He opens the Kingdom and the house of His Father to whom He wills and shuts it in the face of the one who does not deserve it.

The key of David also comes as an allusion and symbol of the sign of the Cross, which opens to the one who signs himself with it in faith the eyes of the person to the Kingdom, and closes the heart and the senses before Satan and his offers.

It can also be said that this key symbolizes the authority given to the Church (Mt 16:19), which is called the authority of binding and loosing, for she alone is the extension of the authority of her Master Christ in opening her doors to repentant sinners and closing them before those who persisted in their error.

A little strength: that is, little power, and it is a reference to the small number of people in this church because of the earthquakes or its meager material means, and it can also be said that it is a reference to the weak health of its bishop, so that his bodily strength became little.

Since this church had no fame or strong reputation, the Lord Christ began His talk with it with great encouragement; He first presented Himself to it as the possessor of authority (v. 7), and now He gives it the good news that He has opened before it the door of the Kingdom, which no one can shut, and He also praises in the bishop and his church their faith, shown in keeping the commandments of God and doing them and holding to the name of God in the most difficult circumstances.

Our beloved God, we thank You from the depths of our hearts for Your love and Your encouragement of us, for we are all possessors of a little strength, very little, and without You we cannot open a door or shut a door, but it is Your promises that fill our hearts with hope.. so come also, my Master, and complete Your work to the full in the life of each one of us and make us hold fast Your name and Your commandments always.

Which say they are Jews, and are not: that is, those who claim religiousness and zeal and are not so. See (ch. 2:9). This applies now to all who have departed from the sound faith and claimed that they are Christians, such as the Jehovah's Witnesses and the Adventists and others, who have no aim except to rob the believers from the Church of God... and Christ describes all these here as a synagogue of Satan since they have become his soldiers and the carriers out of his will against the Church. I will make them to come and worship: another encouragement to the Church not to fear these enemies, for Christ alone is able to crush them and humble them and scatter their counsels under the feet of His Church, and they will see and be sure of My love for you and My protection of your church.
The word of my patience: an expression meaning that you held to My word in the time of trials and your difficult circumstances.

I also will keep thee... the hour of temptation: since you were faithful in the first temptation and held to the faith, you will also be kept and protected from the temptation coming upon the whole world, and what is meant by it is the violent Roman persecution in the time of this church... and this promise can also be generalized to the Church in every time in the face of all persecutions, as long as she is faithful in keeping the commandment of God and shows partiality to no one or accepts a strange faith.

Behold, I come quickly: this expression is repeated more than once and means a warning to the negligent of the coming of the just judgment and an encouragement to those who strive and stand firm in their faith.. (see ch. 2:5). Hold that fast which thou hast: stand firm in what you are in and take care lest it be lost, for God's praise and encouragement of us does not mean the guarantee of our salvation, because if we are careless and neglect our salvation we do not escape God's punishment and His just judgment and we lose the Kingdom of Heaven (Heb 2:3).

My beloved brother... the previous verse warns all of us against losing the free salvation that Christ offered us, for our accepting salvation does not mean the attainment of eternity; remember Judas who lost his crown, which the Apostle Matthias took in his place, and remember also the birthright which the negligent Esau neglected and the watchful Jacob took, and likewise Demas, the disciple of Paul, who lost everything by his attachment to the present world (2 Tim 4:10).
Will I make a pillar: as for the one who overcomes and is victorious, his place will be fixed, "a pillar," and near to Me and to My Father "in the temple of my God."
He shall go no more out: that is, whoever reaches eternity has no chance of going out of it again.
I will write upon him the name: that is, I declare plainly his belonging to Me, to My Father and to the Kingdom of Heaven, so that his glory is declared before all.
The name of my God... the name of the city of my God: this expression may cause confusion for some, for how can Christ have a God, calling Him by the title my God?!

What is meant is that the incarnate Christ, as a representative of humanity and as the firstborn among many brethren, calls God "my God," and this is a wonderful humility on His part and a raising of the level of the victorious believers, that Christ should be one of them by His Incarnation and should call God with them his God. And Christ does not mean that He is less than His Father, who gave Him the title God, and the proof is in the following:
1- It is He who said, "I and my Father are one" (Jn 10:30). "He that hath seen me hath seen the Father" (Jn 14:9).
2- The Holy Spirit bore witness to Him: "and the Word was God" (Jn 1:1).

3- In the Book of Revelation itself: "I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the ending" (Rev 1:8). "I am the first and the last" (Rev 1:17). "I am he which searcheth the reins and hearts: and I will give unto every one of you according to your works" (Rev 2:23). "He that openeth, and no man shutteth; and shutteth, and no man openeth" (Rev 3:7). And finally, which confirms the equality in the interpretation of the verse we are dealing with, Christ will write His name on "the one who overcomes" just as He will write the name of His Father on him, and this is sufficient proof of the equality of the two names in honor and glory. And let us return once more to the reward in its spiritual understanding... whoever is victorious and overcomes, his reward will be the name of God declared in him, and He is the founder of the heavenly city of Jerusalem, and he also receives the name of the city since he has become an eternal citizen in it, and likewise receives the name of Christ its King.
It is the same phrase that the Lord Christ used in all His letters to all the churches.

The church of the Laodiceans: the city of Laodicea was the richest of the seven churches and lay between the cities of Colossae and Philadelphia, and was famous for the wool trade, and it took its name from the name of "Laodice," the wife of Antiochus II.. and the material wealth of this church was the cause of its spiritual problem, as we shall see.
The angel of the church: in the first age it was succeeded by Aurelius the bishop and then Sapharius the bishop and martyr.
These things saith the Amen: "the Amen" here is a title belonging to God alone, and it comes in the meaning of the truth or the One who declares the truth.

The faithful and true witness: since the problem of this church was spiritual lukewarmness, and most of the Lord Christ's letter to it is warning and rebuke... the Lord Christ presented Himself here as the witness and examiner of all works, and when He judges, His judgment is final because He is faithful and true; He is not like men, who lack information when they judge, or whose consciences may differ because of partiality or inclinations when judging someone. The beginning of the creation of God: that is, the head, owner and originator of all creation, as St. John said in his Gospel, "All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made" (Jn 1:3).

Because this church suffers from spiritual lukewarmness, God declares to it that He is the truth and the true, the head and originator of all creatures, and He is the just One who searches everything and does not accept this slackness.

Abundance of money was the basic cause of the slackness of the church of Laodicea, so it sought material pleasure and a life of luxury and left the royal way, which is carrying the cross behind its Master, and fell into spiritual lukewarmness.

Thou art neither cold nor hot: a specific divine diagnosis of the sickness of this church, for it is not in spiritual fervor and the spirituality of worship, and it is not cold either in the sense that it does not acknowledge its sin and feel it. I would thou wert cold or hot: for he who confesses and admits his coldness, that is, his sins, may have stirred in him longings of repentance toward God, as happened with Zacchaeus and the Samaritan woman and the sinful woman and the Apostle Matthew, who was a tax collector, and he who is hot there is no fear for him... but you are neither this nor that... and the phrase "I would thou wert cold" reveals to us the seriousness of lukewarmness and spiritual deception, for before God it is worse than a life of sin itself, because the lukewarm person is deceived about himself and content with what he is in, so he does not offer repentance.

The Lord used here a material expression to bring the sin of lukewarmness and the state of the lukewarm person closer to our minds.. for just as there are foods that are eaten hot (warm), and kinds that are eaten cold and are palatable, the lukewarm food is what the soul does not accept but spits out.. so the lukewarm person has no taste before God.

The Lord Christ makes clear here the cause of the sickness and sin of lukewarmness, for self-regard and wealth entered the heart of this church, and it felt its distinction among the churches and slipped into boasting in its wealth and relied on it, so that it did not feel its real need for God its Savior.
And knowest not that thou art: but the truth is that you are not as you see yourself but as I judge you, and I judge you (O lukewarm one) as being:
Wretched: from wretchedness, that is, you have no real happiness and inner joy in spite of your wealth.

Miserable: because you gave up your divine fellowship and became wretched and in a bad state here and perishing there (eternity). Poor: what is meant is spiritual poverty, in contrast to the church of Smyrna, which was materially poor and whose spiritual riches the Lord praised.
Blind: that is, you do not see the truth of your condition.
Naked: since you did without My grace and relied on what you have, My grace left you and you became naked, without grace, in want, and you find nothing to cover you before Me.

I counsel thee: that is, I offer you a remedy... and it is to be noted that the word "counsel" means that God offers advice to all but does not compel anyone to accept it.. but the person must bear the consequences of his choices... by accepting or rejecting the commandments of God.

To buy of me gold: the first of the three remedies that the Lord offered to this church; I alone am the source of giving, so leave the gold of the earth that you rely on, for nothing came of it but your distance and your lukewarmness, for I am the only source of your wealth... and the gold refined in the fire signifies the richness of the spiritual life, and it also signifies Christ Himself, since He alone is the pure gold refined by the fire of the Cross to offer us salvation. White raiment: the second remedy, which is that you must join and be clothed with inner purity, so that you may not be ashamed of your nakedness before Me on the Day of Judgment.

Anoint thine eyes with eyesalve: that is, respond to the calls and rebukes of the Holy Spirit, for He is responsible for the spiritual insight of a person, and for this reason one of the titles of the Holy Spirit in our Church is "the Spirit of enlightenment."
The summary: the remedy for the sin of lukewarmness can be summarized in the following..
1- Taking refuge in God and declaring my spiritual poverty, so that I acquire God Himself (the refined gold).
2- Striving for purity of heart, without which no one will see Christ.
3- Listening to, responding to and obeying the Holy Spirit of God in our lives, and obeying the commandment and guidance of the Fathers.

Since the Lord's words to this bishop and this church were severe words and a hard warning, He returns here and makes clear that the cause of all His words is love, for just as a father disciplines his children, sometimes even with severe rebuke, all he hopes for is their repentance and their return from their error so that they may enjoy life with him and not lose their salvation, and St. Paul also affirms this meaning in his Epistle to the Hebrews, "whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth" (Heb 12:6). Be zealous therefore, and repent: that is, you must care for the salvation of your soul and exert effort in that, and return by repentance to your first way of life.

Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: a very beautiful picture which makes clear what was explained before, that God respects the will of man and so does not open the door by force, and it also pictures God's longsuffering and patience with us, for He still stands hoping that the person will answer His calls and open to Him (Song 5:2). If any man hear... and open: it is not enough for a person to hear the voice of God and the visitation of His grace to him, but he must rise and open, that is, strive with a sincere will and leave his laziness so that Christ may reign over his house, that is, his heart. I will sup with him, and he with me: he shares with Christ one meal, and this oneness is accomplished by partaking of the Body and Blood of Christ and being satisfied with His holy word.
How wonderful is Your love for me, Lord, that supper with me, the sinner, has become the desire of Your heart (Lk 22:

15) "You are the One who stands hoping to enter so that I may open my heart, and You become all mine and I wholly Yours, and the table of Your unlimited love gathers us... is this not what You offer me every day on Your holy altar... O that I would always open my heart with repentance so that You, Bridegroom of my soul, may enter and sup with me and never leave me...

To sit with me in my throne: this is the reward of the repentant one who overcomes when he is rid of his lukewarmness, for Christ promises him a reward that exceeds every thought and every imagination! ... for how can we sit with God in His throne, that is, in the glory of His Kingdom!! Is this not a wonderful mystery?... And there is another thing that shows us the power of repentance and its effectiveness... who is it whom Christ will seat with Him... it is the very one He was about to spue out of His mouth; how great are God's mercies and how effective is repentance! He not only forgives sinners but rewards them with what is beyond their expectations or deserving.

Even as I also overcame, and am set down: a final word of encouragement in which the Master urges us to overcome and be victorious, for He passed through sufferings and death and came out victorious, and He gave His believing children also the ability to do this by His support of them. And because He overcame in our body, "be of good cheer; I have overcome the world" (Jn 16:33), we also in Him shall overcome and sit with Him in His throne and the throne of His Father.
He that hath an ear: the usual conclusion of all the letters, that we may hear and do what we have heard.

My beloved brother: the lesson learned from the church of the Laodiceans is not to be preoccupied with material things and boast of them. So we must take care to please the faithful Witness who searches the depths of the heart, instead of spending most of our life trying to please ourselves or to please others at the expense of pleasing our eternity... how serious is the sin of lukewarmness and its punishment... have mercy on us, my God, according to Your great mercy. The throne of God and some of His glory: with the end of the third chapter the first scene of the heavenly vision ends, the scene relating to the pastoral letters to the seven churches; as for the fourth and fifth chapters, they serve as an introduction that carries us to the sixth chapter, where the opening of the seven seals begins, and what the fourth chapter deals with is a description of the throne of God and His glory.
After this: that is, after the previous talk and vision about the seven churches.
A door was opened in heaven: spiritually it means the opening of the spirit to see new spiritual things that were closed to all men.

This verse reminds us of the opening of heaven before Stephen at the time of his martyrdom (Acts 7:56) and the ladder that Jacob saw, which joined heaven and earth; both Stephen and Jacob saw something of heaven while on earth, but in John's vision he will see heaven from within heaven, and he will also see, while in heaven, successive events that happen on earth.

Since the Church represents heaven on earth, the rite of the Church has continued to forbid the closing of her doors, as a sign that for whoever wants heaven its door is always open, and this rite remained in force and was set aside only by conditions of security.
The first voice: it is the same voice of Christ (ch. 1:10).

Come up hither: that is, that John, and after him the whole Church, may see something of the glory of heaven, and this is what the Master added by saying "and I will shew thee things which must be hereafter," and the basic purpose of God's declaring to us some scenes of the glory of heaven is to encourage us to be constantly attached to it and to look toward it, so that nothing may distract us from it and we lose our place in it.

After the vision of the seven letters, Christ spoke to John and declared to him a new vision, as he entered through an open door into heaven to see what would happen after the vision of the seven churches.

Immediately I was in the spirit: St. John declared before that he was in the Spirit (ch. 1:10), and now he declares here that he became in the Spirit, meaning that God gave him a new spiritual sense with his transfer to heaven, a sense that fits the new scene he was about to see, and so also every person who listens to the voice of the Master, as John heard, God gives him a distinctive spiritual feeling that is hard for a person to describe to others.

One sat on the throne: human language with all its vocabulary did not help St. John to describe the divine Self, but what God permitted him to see was One sitting on a throne, and this scene accords with our describing heaven as the kingdom of God (that is, His kingdom) and also points to the absolute authority of the One who sits on this throne.
St. John will use the expression "him that sat on the throne" often in the coming chapters.

As for the appearance of this One who sat on the throne, He was to look upon like a jasper stone, white and transparent, as an expression of God's simplicity and purity, and likewise the sardine stone is red like fire, so it signifies the justice of God, and He is steadfast in His covenants with men, as the memorial of the covenant of the rainbow (Gen 9:13) which He gave to Noah after the Flood and to all mankind, that He would not drown them again with a flood, while the green emerald points to God being the source of all life and growth. And all these things (the jasper, the sardine stone and the rainbow) point to the splendor of the glory of God.

The four and twenty seats: John saw twenty-four thrones for heavenly beings around the throne of the One who sits, that is, God made them partners in His council, which is a very special kind of honor.

Four and twenty elders: who are they: we prefer to use the expression heavenly beings, an expression that includes their being distinguished angels or something greater than the angels, as many of the Fathers said. Elders: the Greek origin of this word means priests, so the correct translation of it is priests and not elders.

Four and twenty: this number signifies the completeness of the Church in her two covenants before God (the twelve tribes of the Old Testament and the twelve apostles of the New Testament), and the twenty-four priests represent the priesthood standing before God, which intercedes for the believers and conveys their prayers to God (Rev 5:8), and the white garments they wear represent their purity (like the tunic of the priest and the deacon), while the crowns of gold signify the glory and honor of this exalted rank before God, since He made them like kings, and the Coptic people in general are distinguished by their reverence and respect for the priesthood and its ranks because of the loftiness of its work, since it is the sacrament that completes all the sacraments of the Church, and it has its honor before God.
Note: the Church keeps the feast of the twenty-four priests on the 24th of Hathor, and asks for their intercession and remembers them in her Midnight Praise.

Lightnings and thunderings and voices: these phenomena are connected with the divine presence and point to it, since they were repeated on Mount Sinai at the giving of the Law (Ex 19:16), and all of them make us feel awe and trembling when standing before God, and remembering such things helps a person to resist evil thoughts (wandering of mind) at the time of prayer.

Seven lamps of fire burning: a reference to the Holy Spirit, fiery and giving light, for the Apostle goes on to say "which are the seven Spirits of God"; see (ch. 1:12); it also points to His work in the seven sacraments of the Church. It can also be said that the "lightnings" represent God's gentle, shining promises, while the thunderings represent His awesome warnings, and the voices express His speech and His will declared in creation.

A sea of glass like unto crystal: in the Old Testament and in Solomon's temple there was "a molten sea" (1 Kgs 7:23) and it was for purification.. and now we are before a sea of crystal glass that signifies Baptism in its purity and cleanness, and this sea is before God because no one will see God unless he passes through this Baptism (Jn 3:5). Four beasts full of eyes: what is meant by four beasts is that they are four living beings, and all the Fathers agreed in their interpretations that they are the orders of angels known as the Seraphim and Cherubim, and to complete the explanation about them we will clarify that in the interpretation of verses (7-9).

How beautiful, wonderful and awesome is the scene of heaven that lifts us and raises us to contemplate the glory of God and His throne, so that we long for constant meeting with Him... I beseech You, my God, grant us a share in seeing You as John saw You, and give us the good will to complete our striving in peace.

entries.section: (2) The description of the four beasts and their work

paragraphs.text: 1- Full of eyes: that is, distinguished by God's universal knowledge and many other things that God reveals to them, and these eyes within (v. 8) are also a proof of strong inner knowledge.

entries.section: (2) The description of the four beasts and their work

paragraphs.text: 2- Their visible forms: like a lion... like a calf... a face as a man... like a flying eagle.

(a) The tradition of the Church from of old has taken the forms of these angelic beings as symbols of the four Gospels: the lion points to the Gospel of St. Mark because it begins with a crying voice, and the lion has been linked with the image of St. Mark; the likeness of the calf points to the Gospel of St. Luke because he spoke most about the sacrifices; the face of a man points to St. Matthew because he begins by mentioning the human genealogy of Christ; and the likeness of the eagle points to the Gospel of St. John because he soars in the theological matters and spoke of them much.
(b) Because these creatures are angelic, their forms also indicate their work and their standing.
The lion: a symbol of the strength and power of the angels.
The calf: patience in carrying out difficult tasks.
The man: a proof of intellectual perception and discernment.
The eagle: speed, far-sightedness and loftiness of height.

(c) We can also say that they represent the completeness of creation before God, considering that man is the most important of the rational beings, the lion the noblest of the beasts of prey, the calf represents the tame and self-giving animals, and the eagle is the strongest in the kingdom of birds, so that creation of all kinds stands before God at all times offering Him praise and worship; the four beasts intercede for all creatures.

entries.section: (2) The description of the four beasts and their work

paragraphs.text: 3- Six wings: the wings point to the swift movement of the angels in carrying out the will of God, and they also signify the awe of the sight of God and the glory of His honor, for they fly with two wings, and in reverence and modesty cover their feet with two wings, and in humility veil their faces with two wings (Isa 6:2), and this is what we also remember of them in the prayer of the Gregorian Liturgy.

entries.section: (2) The description of the four beasts and their work

paragraphs.text: Their work: it can be said that their most important and perhaps only work is offering "glory and honour and thanks" to God, declaring with their voices the hymn of sanctification "Holy, holy, holy," which is the same hymn that Isaiah saw in his vision (Isa 6), and which the Church took and added to all her prayers and hymns (the prayer of the Agpeya and the Divine Liturgy). We have nothing better than to pray to God as the angels praise Him, glorify Him and utter His name.

Their prayer also includes praising God in His attributes: He is Almighty (the Sustainer of all and the Creator of things out of nothing), and He is also the eternal, the One who is, and the everlasting, whose kingdom has no end.
5- The Church keeps the feast of the four incorporeal beasts and asks for their intercession, in acknowledgment of their standing and the loftiness of their work, on the 8th of Hathor.

My beloved sister, if the angels, who have spiritual bodies of light, cover themselves with their wings before God out of modesty and sanctification of His honor and awe, should we not learn, and teach our children from childhood, the virtue of modesty in our clothing, and likewise covering the head and reverence during the times of prayer?! How sweet it is to stand with awe and reverence before God.

entries.section: (3) The hymn of the twenty-four priests

paragraphs.text: When Isaiah heard the angels chanting "Holy.. holy.. holy," the posts of the door of the temple and its foundations shook and he was terrified and cried out, "Woe is me.. for I am a man of unclean lips" (Isa 6:3-5), and here we are before an exactly similar scene.. so when the four incorporeal beasts uttered the name of the holy God, what happened?!!

Fall down... and worship: the twenty-four priests could not bear the cry of the name of the holy God, so they immediately prostrated themselves in reverence, submission and contrition before the declaration of the glory of God.
Cast their crowns: since their crowns were a kind of honor that God gave them, they return it to Him, as though saying that You alone are the possessor of honor.

And notice, beloved, that in the rite of the liturgy of our Church the bishop enters the church with the crown of his priesthood, but at the reading of the Gospel, and even before it, at the hymn of Agios, the high priest removes his head covering, as though imitating this heavenly scene and declaring that there is no honor except to the one God who sits on His throne... and he completes the whole prayer of the Liturgy without putting the crown on again.

entries.section: (3) The hymn of the twenty-four priests

paragraphs.text: Here the twenty-four priests offer a hymn to the Lord God in which they declare that He alone is worthy of glory and honor, because He is Almighty and the Owner of all creation and its Maker by His word and will... and this praise includes us human beings, for we are God's creation and the work of His hands... that is, we are remembered before God in the hymn of the heavenly ones.
Do you feel this, beloved... and do you share with the heavenly ones in the divine praise?

The prayers of the Church's Midnight Praise are among the sweetest prayers that lift the heart to God, so have you enjoyed them? May you share in them with the Church, so that you may be with the heavenly ones in their high spiritual feelings.
The sealed book and the hymn of the Lamb
And I saw: that is, a new scene and sight which St. John adds to the scene in the previous chapter.

In the right hand of him that sat: the right hand signifies honor, and the book here is the Holy Bible, and the indication that it is in the right hand means the lofty standing of the word of God and the duty of reading it and doing its commandments. Within and on the backside: books were written on one side and then rolled up in the form of a cylinder, but his saying that it was written within and on the backside means:
First: the abundance of what is written and its richness, on the one hand.
Second: that there are apparent meanings and others deep and hidden in the word of God.
Sealed with seven seals: that is, this book is rolled up and closed upon itself and has upon it seven seals that signify...
1- The firmness of its closing, and that God is the keeper of His word.
2- The seals also signify God's covenants with men, since all the ancient treaties were not reckoned valid unless they were sealed with the seals of the king.
3- They also signify the hidden and symbolic meanings, which need Christ, who alone is able to open them, and His Holy Spirit declares their mysteries to all men.
