Freely: that is, a gift and grace from God, and this is in keeping with His love and fatherhood, for salvation was offered freely and all His graces to us are free, and likewise His spiritual gifts, but let us not forget that God is also just and does not forget all who rejected righteousness and sought evil.

entries.section: (1) The dwelling of God with men

paragraphs.text: He that overcometh: this expression was used in (ch. 2, ch. 3) with the letters to the bishops of the seven churches, and as a reminder here we say that this expression means:
a) The possibility of victory that was given by salvation to the children of God.

b) The necessity of victory for the inheritance and the enjoyment of the free gifts (the fountain of the water of life). Shall inherit all things: what God has prepared for His children who love His holy name and who overcome by the patience of their faith and their striving. I will be his: the Lord Christ moved here to the particularity of the relationship between each overcoming soul and its Christ, for after the discussion had been about the Christian people, "they shall be his people" (v. 3..), the words here are directed to each overcoming soul individually, so that the whole inheritance (all of heaven) becomes for each one, and every person becomes a distinguished son, as if he were an only son enjoying the fullness of his father's fatherhood ... and let us also notice the gentleness of Christ's expression in describing the relationship when He said "I will be his God," for He did not say he will be my servant but said son, which is the expression most in keeping with the fatherhood of God, who gives the inheritance not to slaves but to sons.

entries.section: (1) The dwelling of God with men

paragraphs.text: This verse makes clear the categories of those barred from the eternal inheritance and from the free gift of the water of life, whose portion is not in the heavenly Jerusalem but their destruction, "the second death," and endless torment in the lake burning with fire and brimstone... and these categories are:

(1) The fearful: what is meant here is not fear in the sense of anxiety for others or fear of animals or insects ... but what is meant is those who feared the world and the wicked, so they denied Christ and abandoned the faith for the sake of earthly life.
(2) Unbelieving: those who refused to believe in Christ and His free redemption and resisted His Church, for without faith it is impossible to please Him.
(3) The abominable: those who commit sins of impurity and did not repent of them.

(4) Sorcerers: those who used magic and the powers of evil and darkness and by this departed from God and became His enemy. (5) All liars: that is, those who went astray and led people astray ... and instead of doing the truth (the will of God in their lives) they did a lie (that is, they lied to themselves and to others.) And whoever lived his life in lying is none other than a child of the devil, for the Lord Christ says of Satan, "When he speaketh a lie, he speaketh of his own: for he is a liar, and the father of it" (Jn 8:44). (6) Idolaters: in its direct sense, whoever bows down to and worships idols, but in its spiritual meaning it is everyone who worships and clings to self or money..

God's love and fatherhood do not forget your weariness on earth and will compensate you for it with glories in heaven that cannot be expressed, so hold fast to your spiritual striving and endure the temporary pains of earth and do not be drawn after passing desires, and you will obtain the glories of heaven.

entries.section: (2) A description of the city of God (the New Jerusalem)

paragraphs.text: An angel appeared and spoke with St. John, whom the saint recognized in the Spirit, and he pointed out to us that he was one of the angels who carried the seven bowls of God's wrath (ch. 15), and the angel here was commissioned with a new mission, which is to show St. John the heavenly city. Just as this angel proclaimed God's justice in punishing the wicked with the bowls, here he proclaims God's justice in rewarding the righteous. He called the heavenly city the bride, as came in (v. 2), and declared that her bridegroom is Christ, a strong reference to the union of Christ (the Bridegroom) with His triumphant Church (the bride), and the angel used the name the Lamb here because it fits the Redeemer Bridegroom who bought the salvation of His Church with His blood.

entries.section: (2) A description of the city of God (the New Jerusalem)

paragraphs.text: He carried me away in the spirit: and this is in keeping with the state of St. John throughout the vision.
A great and high mountain: the expression here is symbolic, for it is customary among people to climb high summits so as to see the scene completely and comprehensively.

The purpose of the angel's taking St. John was to see the city in detail from all its sides and dimensions, and therefore the vision was from a high place so that nothing would escape him, and being high on the mountain symbolizes rising above earthly material things, because the heavenly city is entirely spiritual. And St. John repeats the same thing that came in (v. 2), that it is coming down from heaven from God (see the explanation).

entries.section: (2) A description of the city of God (the New Jerusalem)

paragraphs.text: Most precious stone: the greatest and most splendid stone.

Because of the intense beauty of the city (the heavenly Jerusalem), St. John could not portray this beauty for us in the limited language of men, so he used the expression "having the glory of God," that is, because it is His city and His Church and the place prepared before the foundation of the world for the children of God who inherit, and because it is the making of God Himself and His preparation, he ascribed to it His indescribable and unlimited glory, so that her honor is from the honor of God, and her standing and beauty surpass all imagination. And he added that it was very bright, with the brightness of a precious stone like the diamond in our present time, and this stone was also mentioned in the discussion of the throne of God (ch. 4:3), and the transparent, pure stone in its symbolic meaning indicates the purity of the Church's teaching and her firm faith and the virtues of her saints.

entries.section: (2) A description of the city of God (the New Jerusalem)

paragraphs.text: A wall great and high: the wall here has more than one significance or meaning:
1- It signifies God's surrounding of His redeemed people in the city Himself, for God is the fortress and the refuge (Ps 43:2).
2- The wall also signifies the one and only Church, for one wall surrounds the whole of the one city.
3- The height of the wall, "high," signifies the exalted standing of the city, since in ancient times the greatness of cities was measured by the height and breadth of their walls.
Twelve gates: this statement agrees with what Ezekiel also mentioned in his vision (Ezek 48:31-34), and the existence of twelve gates (three gates on each side) is a reference to:
1- The breadth of God's mercies, for if the way of striving on earth has a narrow gate, the heavenly reward has gates wide and spacious.
2- The acceptance of the Gentiles from all races and from all quarters of the earth.
3- The gates, like the wall, give a sense of security and guarding.

"Twelve angels": God put an angel at each gate, and this reminds us of "the overshadowing cherubim" on the ark of the covenant, and the presence of angels at the gates symbolizes care, protection and overshadowing for the people of God. The names of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel: a reference to the entrance of the believers and saints of the Old Testament into this city, for God kept His covenant with His people and everyone who was faithful among them has a gate by which to enter eternity. The general meaning of the two verses (12, 13) is the acceptance of all believers from every direction and their enjoyment of the particular presence of God, "their wall," and the service of the angels to them.

entries.section: (2) A description of the city of God (the New Jerusalem)

paragraphs.text: Just as the believers of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel were accepted, so also the believers of the Church of the New Testament will be accepted, and everyone who received and took over the faith from the Fathers the twelve Apostles and from the Church. Twelve foundations: the names of the twelve tribes were written (v. 12) on the gates of the city, while the names of the Fathers the Apostles were the foundations carrying the city, and this is a clear reference that the foundation of the building of this heavenly city and of entering it is faith in Christ Himself, which was the foundation of the good news and preaching of the pure Apostles, and this is in keeping with what St. Paul the Apostle mentioned: "And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone; in whom all the building fitly framed together) "... Eph 2:20, 21.

entries.section: (2) A description of the city of God (the New Jerusalem)

paragraphs.text: In (ch. 11) St. John was given a reed to measure the temple of God and the altar, but the one who measures here is the accompanying angel, and the purpose of the measuring is to highlight the glory, splendor and breadth of the city. A golden reed: the reed is the unit of measurement (like the meter), and its being of gold is to indicate the dignity of the city whose dimensions will be measured. There is another beautiful meaning, which is that spiritual (golden) things are measured only by spiritual things (a reed of gold.)

entries.section: (2) A description of the city of God (the New Jerusalem)

paragraphs.text: As for the description of the city as St. John saw it (and of course these are all spiritual, symbolic measurements and not truly material), it was foursquare, that is, the splendor of her glory is equal if a person looks at her from any side, and so is her height.
The furlong: about 185 meters.

Twelve thousand furlongs: the material measure (two thousand two hundred and twenty kilometers) has no value here, but the purpose is to leave the reader's imagination to grasp the breadth of this city.

entries.section: (2) A description of the city of God (the New Jerusalem)

paragraphs.text: As for the height of her wall, it was (144 thousand cubits), and the number "144,000" has been repeated in the book twice, in (ch. 7:4) the number of "the sealed," and (ch. 14:1) "the followers of the Lamb," and in both cases this number was a figure for multitude, because it is the product of the numbers of perfection (12 x 12 x 1000), and consequently the height of the wall of the city here is a figure for the height of her glory beyond the imagination of any man.

The measure of a man, that is, of the angel: the human cubit equals about 50 cm, but the one who did the measuring is the angel, so the meaning intended is a spiritual one, that is, the great height and loftiness of this city.

entries.section: (2) A description of the city of God (the New Jerusalem)

paragraphs.text: After St. John mentioned that the foundations of the city are twelve foundations (the Apostles of Christ), he begins in the verses that follow to describe each foundation of them in terms of the stone it is made of and its color, with the meaning and spiritual reflections this carries.

First came in (v. 18) the general description, for the wall was of a precious stone, bright like the diamond, "jasper" (v. 11), and it is crystalline, that is, transparent, and likewise the city was of gold, which is a very precious metal, "pure," that is, without impurities or additions that reduce its value, but it is also not ordinary gold, for it is gold transparent as glass, in the sense that the brightness of the city and her glory does not hide or distract man from seeing God Himself. The first foundation, jasper: a transparent, shining stone inclining somewhat to green, and by its brightness and transparency it signifies the upright faith, and in its greenness eternal life.
The second foundation, sapphire: it signifies that the city is spiritual and heavenly and not subject to earthly measures.
The third foundation, chalcedony: a white stone that signifies purity and cleanness.
The fourth foundation, emerald: a green stone that signifies growth in grace.
The fifth foundation, sardonyx: it is white streaked with red, a symbol that purity is founded on the blood of Christ.

The sixth foundation, sardius: that is, it is built on the mystery of Christ's redemption (His precious blood.) The seventh foundation, chrysolite: the purest kind of gold, for everything in it does not rust (does not change or end.) The eighth foundation, beryl: it is the color of the calm, clear sea, and this is the state of the dwellers of the city of God. The ninth foundation, topaz: the topaz signifies enlightened insight.

The tenth foundation, chrysoprasus: life and its permanence (eternity.) The eleventh foundation, jacinth: sky blue, and its stone is very hard, a symbol of the immortality of the city and its dwellers.

The twelfth foundation, amethyst: a stone of purple color (dark red.) These stones and their colors have carried many spiritual reflections for many interpreters, but all agreed that nothing was meant by these stones except to highlight the wealth, virtue and grace that distinguish the city.

entries.section: (2) A description of the city of God (the New Jerusalem)

paragraphs.text: The foundations of the city (various stones) came as a reference to the various virtues that those who enter it must bear, but the gates came alike, a reference to the fact that entrance is by the one door of the sheep, single in its attributes.
The pearl: it is the stone hidden in the shell of the sea, and it signifies here the splendor of the glory of God that shines on the gates of the city, which had been hidden from us and has appeared.

The street of the city: that is, its middle and center, and it came like the description of her wall in (v. 18), that is, the gathering of the believers in it in great glory, which is symbolized by precious gold.
And in other translations the phrase "the street of the city" came in the sense of its square.

entries.section: (2) A description of the city of God (the New Jerusalem)

paragraphs.text: The temple is the symbol of God's presence and dwelling, and God in truth is not limited by a made or created place, and consequently there is no need for a temple, for in the heavenly New Jerusalem God the Father will always dwell, and His Son (the Lamb) will stand in His glory in her midst, and for this St. John used the expression that "the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are the temple of it," that is, God shepherds His children in the Kingdom as a tender Father and as the Savior and Redeemer who loved them to death.

entries.section: (2) A description of the city of God (the New Jerusalem)

paragraphs.text: In the same way that he said that a temple is of no use, there will also be no sun or moon, first because they are among the requirements of earthly, temporal life and the old life that has ended, and second because there is no need of any light, since God is also her light and her splendor.

entries.section: (2) A description of the city of God (the New Jerusalem)

paragraphs.text: By the light of it: that is, the divine light of the city..

The children of God enjoy His light and walk, that is, grow in His knowledge and love, and this wonderful heavenly scene agrees with what Isaiah also mentioned: "And the nations shall walk in thy light, and kings in the brightness of thy rising ... they all gather themselves together, they come to thee" (Isa 60:3-5). The kings of the earth: the saints also come bearing their virtues and their former sufferings for the sake of faith, "their glory and honor."

entries.section: (2) A description of the city of God (the New Jerusalem)

paragraphs.text: Because God is her sun that never sets, there will be no darkness or night after this, nor any need to shut her gates.. for the gates were shut in earthly time to protect man from his enemies and to guard him from the fears of darkness, but now none of the old things has any place. The glory and honor of the nations: that is, the praise and glorification of all peoples and all nations for the name of the living, holy God.

entries.section: (2) A description of the city of God (the New Jerusalem)

paragraphs.text: There shall in no wise enter into it: of course, after the general judgment, the expression "shall in no wise enter into it" is meant to say that there will not be in her, for everyone who was "defiled or abominable" has his fate in the lake burning with fire and brimstone ... but the expression also carries to the reader a final reminder of the necessity of constant repentance on earth, for there is no place in the city for unrepentant sinners.

They which are written in the Lamb's book of life: that is, those whom the Lord Christ called to eternal salvation and who accepted this salvation and completed their striving and struggle against evil to the end, so that they have the great inheritance.

My beloved God, in Your love for us You wished to show a glimpse of the beauty of eternity and the splendor of the life that lasts with You and in Your presence, and despite the beauty of this glimpse, our human mind is still too limited to understand or imagine everything, but we trust in what St. Paul declared to us, that "Eye hath not seen ... which it is not lawful for a man to utter" (1 Cor 2:9, 2 Cor 12:4). I thank You, my God, for what Your hands have prepared for me even if I do not understand it now, but with St. Paul I desire that place and I desire to be with You always, for I believe that it is "far better" (Phil 1:23). The tree of life and the conclusion of the book: introduction to the chapter: verses (1-6) come completing the description of the city whose description began in the preceding chapter, while the remaining verses (7-21) come as the conclusion of the book and its various prophecies.
A pure river: not like the rivers of the world, which are clear at times and muddied at other times.
Clear as crystal: to stress its clarity and purity.

The meaning is of course spiritual, for there is no thirst and no drinking in the Kingdom of God. What is meant by the river and the water of life is the sweet divine consolations granted by God to His chosen ones, to those who love Him and to the heirs of eternity. For this reason he said that the source of the river is proceeding out of the throne. This description reminds us of the conversation of the Lord Christ with the Samaritan woman about the water of life, which whoever drinks of it shall never thirst (Jn 4:14).
In the midst of the street of it: an expression meaning the place that is open to all.
On either side: on both banks of the river.

St. John saw "the tree of life" on either side of the river. Some have held that this means a number of trees. But because the meaning is spiritual and symbolic in the first place, and because he used the expression "tree" and not "trees," we find that the meaning intended is that this tree is available and satisfying to all who dwell in the city, wherever their position on either side of the river.

The tree of life: most interpreters of the Holy Bible agree that the tree of life, available to all, is one of the expressions concerning the Lord Christ Himself, for He is the source of satisfaction for all who hunger and thirst after righteousness (Mt 5:6). Some have also held that the tree of life may be a type of the Cross.

And this "tree," that is, Christ, is abundant in gifts and graces to His children, and gives to them every month. He is not like the seasonal tree whose giving and fruit come once in the year, which is an indication of the continual satisfaction of the believers in their God. The expression "twelve manner of fruits" points to the richness, perfection and variety of these gifts. Since the year in our earthly understanding comprises twelve months, this means continuity throughout the year, that is, in the Kingdom forever.

And the leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations: it is customary that the leaves of trees are gathered to be burned, but in the tree of life there is nothing unprofitable. Even its leaves are a source of consolation and rest, "healing," and the whole meaning is of course symbolic. By the nations are meant the believers from all the world, and not the Jews only.

The dear reader will not miss the contrast between this verse, in which the tree of life has become available to all, and what is said in the Book of Genesis (ch. 2:9), when it was hidden from men because of sin.

Since sin has completely passed away, and there is nothing unclean or defiled in heaven, where God is always present with His people, the first curse, which was because of sin, has also been lifted, and all its consequences, the toil of man and his suffering, have likewise been lifted, for eternal rest has begun. The source of this rest is the permanent presence of Christ "the Lamb." As for the heirs, "His servants," they spend eternity in the service of their God, with continual praise and glorification of His holy name, sharing with the angels in their heavenly work.

And they shall see his face: God said to Moses in ancient times, "there shall no man see me, and live" (Ex 33:20). Here the gift has become ours: after we are rid of the material body and rise with our bodies in a glorified form of light, we are able by it to see God face to face. This is the greatest gift that a spiritual man could desire. St. Paul also referred to this very scene when he said, "For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face" (1 Cor 13:12). His name shall be in their foreheads: an indication of belonging and attachment to God alone.

What is said in this verse agrees with what was explained in the previous chapter (v. 25): the absence of darkness and fear from the city of God, and no need for any created light such as the sun and the moon, because God will be everything to them and will make them need nothing else (see the commentary on ch. 21:25).
And he said unto me: the angel who was speaking to St. John.
These sayings are faithful: that is, everything you have seen and heard is true.

At the end of the scene of the vision of the city of God, the angel concludes his talk with St. John, assuring him that everything he saw and heard in this vision is true and genuine, and that the Lord God, in His good will, wished to reveal some of these scenes to His servants who are striving on earth, to encourage them to stand firm in the striving and resistance in which they are engaged, and so that their resolve may not fail before afflictions. He adds, reassuring them, that the appointed time for these things to happen is near and that its coming will be swift."

Yes, my God, we trust in Your promises, but at times we forget and our hearts become downcast, since we have set our ambition on the passing earth. But blessed is he whose eyes are fixed on heaven and on You, my Father, for he will have joy always here, and longing to meet You in Your heaven... O my God, how I long to see You!! Have mercy on me and make me one of those who have this portion.

entries.section: (2) The conclusion of the book and the announcement of the coming of Christ

paragraphs.text: Behold, I come quickly: the words here are of the Lord Christ concerning His Second Coming.

As the book draws near its end, the Lord Christ reassures those who await Him, announcing His swift coming, and He also commends everyone who believed and whose heart clung to the words of the prophecies of the whole Book of Revelation.

entries.section: (2) The conclusion of the book and the announcement of the coming of Christ

paragraphs.text: I John: the saint pointed to his name to confirm the authority and truthfulness of the Book of Revelation.

Spiritual feelings reached their utmost and filled the being of St. John after all that he had seen and heard, and he found himself (especially after hearing the last voice of Christ) going down on his knees, "I fell down," to worship before the feet of the angel who had been his guide in this vision. But the angel prevented him from doing so, giving the reason: that he (the angel) is of God's creation, which worships Him and glorifies Him like the rest of the prophets and saints, but worship must be offered to God alone.

entries.section: (2) The conclusion of the book and the announcement of the coming of Christ

paragraphs.text: Seal not: do not conceal.

The Lord Christ wanted everything the saint saw in the Book of Revelation to reach us, so the command came to him to declare to us everything he saw. The Lord also urges him to do this quickly, since the time of His coming has become near (v. 7).

entries.section: (2) The conclusion of the book and the announcement of the coming of Christ

paragraphs.text: Christ declares that the time of repentance has ended with the end of earthly time and the beginning of eternity at His Second Coming. So everyone who is "unjust" will be repaid according to what he did, and everyone who defiled his body by sin will remain as he is. There is no longer any room to correct or change conditions... And just as the state of the wicked will remain as it is.. so also the state of the righteous.., for everyone who lived in righteousness, purity and holiness will remain as he was. That is, eternity is an extension of what a person sowed in his life on earth, and this makes clear to us the following truths:
(1) That God's wide mercies have as their sphere the life of man on earth, but what a person dies upon determines his final destiny.
(2) God is perfectly just, and so He repays the wicked and the righteous according to what they have done, without partiality.
(3) This verse carries a warning about the final destiny of man and urges him to repent before opportunities are lost.

entries.section: (2) The conclusion of the book and the announcement of the coming of Christ

paragraphs.text: Behold, I come quickly: what is meant is His Second Coming (v. 7). My reward is with me: this means that I alone am the giver of recompense and repayment, and the Judge (ch. 11:18). To give every man according as his work shall be: this expression is repeated in (Mt 16:27), (Rom 2:6), (ch. 2:22), and it is a proof of the divinity of the Lord Christ, that He is the just Judge.

Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end, the first and the last: these words also came in (ch. 1:8, ch. 21:6), and their meaning is the affirmation of the divine attributes of the Lord Christ, such as that He is the source and Creator of all things and that He is the eternal and everlasting God. He spoke of Himself with such attributes at the beginning of the book, and here He speaks with the very same attributes at its end, to declare to us that it is He who allowed John this vision and that He Himself is its subject and its essence.

entries.section: (2) The conclusion of the book and the announcement of the coming of Christ

paragraphs.text: That they may have right to the tree of life: that is, worthy to enjoy eternal life.

Here comes the promise of lasting happiness for the heirs of eternal life (the tree of life). This worthiness is made to rest on keeping God's commandments and doing them. For entering heaven is not by faith only, but also by striving to carry the commandment into practical life and to do it. This reminds us of what the Lord Christ Himself said: "If ye love me, keep my commandments" (Jn 14:15).

entries.section: (2) The conclusion of the book and the announcement of the coming of Christ

paragraphs.text: As for those driven out, who have no right to enter the city or to come near its gates, they are the dogs: everyone who persecuted the Church with his barking or tore at her flesh.

Sorcerers: everyone who had power through the dragon or the beast (Satan.) Likewise also those whose bodies the lusts have enslaved, such as the fornicators, and those who killed believers or unbelievers, and whoever worshiped anything other than God, whether money or position or self (idols), and whoever loved deceit or misleading or lying... For them there is no place in the city of God.

entries.section: (2) The conclusion of the book and the announcement of the coming of Christ

paragraphs.text: I Jesus: as the Lord said of Himself at the beginning of the book, "The Revelation of Jesus Christ"
(ch. 1:1), He comes here and affirms at the end of the book that the words are still His.
I have sent mine angel: what is meant here is the sending of St. John to us to inform us of what he witnessed and saw. To testify unto you: to inform you of the truth of these things.

I am the root and the offspring of David: that is, I am the Maker of David and his Creator, because I am God the Word, and by my Incarnation I became a man like you, of the offspring of David and his bodily descent.

This verse comes to ratify the whole Book of Revelation and to affirm its soundness. The Lord Christ Himself declares that it is He who allowed John to see all these heavenly visions so that the Church might know them in the various ages. It is He also who sent John to us and commanded him to write them (v. 10).

entries.section: (2) The conclusion of the book and the announcement of the coming of Christ

paragraphs.text: The Spirit: is the Holy Spirit.
The bride: the Church.
Let him that heareth: every believer who hears what the Holy Spirit and the Church declare to him.

The Holy Spirit sets the hearts of the believers on fire, and likewise works powerfully in the Church, so that she bears the same call of the Holy Spirit to her children. All declare their longing for the moments of meeting with Christ and cry out from the depths of their being, "Come," and those who thirst after righteousness take and drink the fullness of the spiritual gifts freely, for the time of their striving and their labors has passed and the time of the divine reward has come.

entries.section: (2) The conclusion of the book and the announcement of the coming of Christ

paragraphs.text: These two verses carry a warning of the utmost severity from the Lord Christ Himself. He affirms, "I testify," that what is in this book, "the prophecy of this book," is His own word, and no human being is permitted to add to it a letter or to take anything from it. Whoever tries to do this, or comes near to attempting it, is subject to the following:
1- The woes of God and His severe punishment, as came with the opening of some of the seals or the seven bowls in the book itself.

2- His name is blotted out of eternity, so that he has no inheritance or portion, but is cast into the outer darkness, where is the lake of fire and brimstone, deprived of all the promises of the Book of Revelation promised to those who love the holy name of God.

entries.section: (2) The conclusion of the book and the announcement of the coming of Christ

paragraphs.text: He which testifieth: is the Lord Jesus Himself.

The Lord Christ, who is the faithful Witness, declares to us here that He responds to the call of the Church and the longing of all His believing children. When they cried out, "Come," His answer came reassuring and responsive, that His coming is certain and swift. Amen. Even so, come, Lord Jesus: as soon as St. John heard these words from the mouth of the Lord of glory, his heart was set aflame and he answered the Lord, not for himself only but on behalf of all the believers, expressing our longings for eternity with his words, "Come, Lord Jesus."

entries.section: (2) The conclusion of the book and the announcement of the coming of Christ

paragraphs.text: St. John concludes his Revelation by invoking the grace of the Lord Jesus (the Giver of all grace) to be with the Church and all her believers in all the days of their earthly striving. After what we have witnessed in this whole book, how much we all need the work of God's grace in our lives, so that we may complete our striving and pass through the difficult times in the fear of God, also set aflame by His love, which always renews our longing to meet Him and to see His glory and the glory of His good Father and the Holy Spirit.

I wish that, amid the crowding of life and the dazzle of material lusts, you would not forget your goal, which is eternal life with Christ. So care for your relationship with God through prayers and spiritual readings, and the Holy Spirit will help you, giving you the Holy Mysteries and supporting you to complete your striving until you enjoy the Kingdom.
May the blessing of the prayers and intercessions of the beloved St. John be with us. Amen.
